Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelids, typically involving the part of the eyelid where the eyelashes grow. It can cause symptoms such as itching, redness, swelling, and crusting around the eyelashes. Blepharitis is often a chronic condition that can be challenging to manage.

There are two main types of blepharitis: anterior and posterior. Anterior blepharitis affects the outside front edge of the eyelid where the eyelashes are attached. Posterior blepharitis affects the inner edge of the eyelid that comes into contact with the eyeball and is often associated with dysfunction of the meibomian glands [1].

Common causes of blepharitis include bacterial infections, particularly by Staphylococcus species, and skin conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis and rosacea [2]. Other contributing factors can include allergies, eyelash mites (Demodex), and poor eyelid hygiene [3].

Treatment for blepharitis typically involves maintaining good eyelid hygiene, such as regular cleaning of the eyelid margins with warm compresses and diluted baby shampoo or commercial lid scrubs. In some cases, topical or oral antibiotics may be prescribed to manage bacterial infections [4]. Additionally, managing underlying conditions like seborrheic dermatitis or rosacea can help control symptoms [5].

full_text:
Blepharitis is a chronic inflammatory process of the eyelid margins [2][3]. It can affect individuals of any age and is characterized by symptoms such as burning sensation, irritation, tearing, photophobia, blurred vision, and red eyes [2]. Blepharitis may be classified into two subtypes based on the anatomic location: anterior and posterior; it can also be categorized based on symptom duration as either acute or chronic [1][3]. 

The exact pathogenesis of blepharitis is not fully understood; however, it is thought to be caused by bacterial colonization (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis) or meibomian gland dysfunction [1][2]. Other contributing factors include allergens and parasitic infestations, such as Demodex mites [1][4]. Common systemic associations include rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis [2].

Diagnosis of blepharitis is primarily based on clinical features as there are no specific diagnostic laboratory tests [3]. Treatment involves long-term eyelid hygiene and may include topical or systemic antibiotics depending on the underlying cause and severity of the condition [3][5]. Although it is not sight-threatening, blepharitis can lead to permanent alterations of the eyelid margin if left untreated [4].
